Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J35/J35nB338.xml). Wondrously Profound Record of Chan Master Kuifu of Lingrui (Nun-Ancestor). Morning roosters and evening bells compress the day's round into a scene of unceasing bustle. Lingrui Kuifu opens an informal address with the pair, then says the twelve hours have pierced the hearers' noses, dragging and tumbling them about until the broad world offers no place to plant a foot. Time cannot be squandered, age and illness do not make appointments, and death defeats boasts of heroism. She urges finding a way to turn and making an effort now, then says more words are useless and asks each person to consider it. The daily sounds become a demand for freedom within time, not a complaint that ordinary temple schedules should simply be abolished.

Senses.Explanation: Morning roosters and evening bells compress the day's round into a scene of unceasing bustle. Lingrui Kuifu opens an informal address with the pair, then says the twelve hours have pierced the hearers' noses, dragging and tumbling them about until the broad world offers no place to plant a foot. Senses.Explanation: After suffering frost and snow, even falling willow catkins make one start. Prior hardship leaves the practitioner sensitive even to a slight new disturbance; masters use the image to answer questions about Chan trials and recognition. Four independent current deployments: Pufuzhuo, Shitian Faxun, Chushi Fanqi, and Tianzhang Yu. Pufuzhuo caps a present sermon; Shitian, Chushi, and Tianzhang answer different current questions directly. The Tier-3 lamp gives Tianzhang’s own exchange, not another recension of the same old case. This is an image of remembered adversity, not a literal claim that willow catkins are dangerous.

Senses.Explanation: Already present, complete, or ready at hand rather than newly produced. Named Chan speakers apply the word to each encountered matter, a public case, immediate use, scenery before the eyes, and everything disclosed in the present scene. Yuanwu Keqin pairs 'this very thing is ready' with 'this very thing is for use'; Ruibai Mingxue asks who lacks what is originally ready, while Hanxiu Xingyun pairs original completeness with everything already present. Chan bends an ordinary word for something ready-made by using it to challenge the search for a result elsewhere, yet the word itself does not tell the reader what the ready thing is in every passage.

Senses.Explanation: A public case that is already complete, present, or ready to hand. The expression is fully attested in Chinese Chan records as a case-term and an utterance. One address says, 'One who comes this way is a ready-made public case.' Another named record subject waits for the assembly to settle, says only that even a ready-made public case cannot be arranged, and steps down. A later record says that whenever an unnamed monk came, Muzhou said, 'Ready-made public case.' Teachers also ask directly what a ready-made public case is and answer with such lines as 'the eastern ravine's water flows into the western ravine; clouds rise on the southern mountain and the northern mountain.' Yuanwu says that before the ready-made public case is spoken its pattern is already manifest, and when its root is raised it leaks through layer after layer. The expression is also followed by 'there is no need to investigate' in fourteen matches across fourteen files. These Chinese uses supply both the literal compound and its use as an actual public-case expression.

Shiyu summons the assembly, says the case is already present and spares them thirty blows, then asks whether they accept it. Acceptance, he says, resembles a worm accidentally making a pattern in wood; nonacceptance raises the problem of retrieving a pearl from the deep. He contrasts stories of obtaining and losing a pearl and asks how truth and falsity, hidden and manifest, can be distinguished. Turning to his present speaking of precepts through Chan teaching and vice versa, he tests all four alternatives and ends with the image of a pure full-moon pearl and an exclamation of grievance. The initial remission is Shiyu's own challenge, not proof that the listeners have passed it.

Acceptance, he says, resembles a worm accidentally making a pattern in wood; nonacceptance raises the problem of retrieving a pearl from the deep. Turning to his present speaking of precepts through Chan teaching and vice versa, he tests all four alternatives and ends with the image of a pure full-moon pearl and an exclamation of grievance. Within the compilation's section for Muzhou Daoming, Muzhou sees a monk and says the case is already present, sparing him thirty blows. The monk answers, 'I am thus.' Muzhou asks why the guardian at the monastery gate raises his fist; the monk replies that the guardian too is thus. Only then does the record say that Muzhou strikes him. The initial remittance and subsequent actual blow are different turns: reading the formula as 'I give you thirty blows' erases that sequence. Senses.Explanation: The case is already present, and the speaker says he spares the recipient thirty blows. Here 'spare' translates the remittance expressed by the Chinese verb; it does not mean that the encounter is finished or that the recipient has been approved. In Muzhou's dialogue the monk answers twice and an actual strike follows. Wanru inserts the formula among short appraisals of older sayings and insists that neither knowing the old cases nor understanding oneself is sufficient alone. Shiyu asks whether the assembly accepts the remittance and turns the issue toward truth and falsity, concealment and manifestation. Danxia places it after Fayan and Xiushan repeat precisely the same words, then comments on not punishing guilt or rewarding merit. These varied surroundings explain why an apparently ready-made case cannot be treated as a fixed verbal solution. The notes distinguish an initial pronouncement about thirty blows from any separately recorded action that follows.

Senses.Note: The witnesses show presentation, reuse, and criticism; they do not establish a single intention behind every use.
